title: Assessing English as a Second Language Middle School Students' Ability to Learn Engineering Concepts
venue: American Society for Engineering Education Annual Conference & Exposition
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether English as a Second Language (ESL) middle school students can learn engineering concepts effectively through hands-on, project-based instruction delivered by engineering teaching fellows. The broader problem addressed is how to teach STEM content to limited-English-proficiency students in ways that also support English vocabulary and academic language development.

The intervention consisted of a sequence of seven one-hour classes at Sherwood Githens Middle School in Durham, North Carolina. Eight sixth-grade ESL students worked through inquiry-based lessons on electric circuits, potential, current, resistance, and motors, using highly scaffolded instruction, visuals, simplified vocabulary, demonstrations, and paired hands-on activities. The unit culminated in building and modifying model electric cars to explore how resistors change speed.

The paper also describes how undergraduate and graduate engineering teaching fellows should be trained for ESL classrooms and how such lesson materials can be prepared for the TeachEngineering digital library. Student learning was assessed with picture-based questions, cloze and multiple-choice items, and performance tasks requiring students to build circuits. The authors conclude that ESL students can make substantial progress in engineering content in a short sequence of carefully scaffolded lessons, while simultaneously practicing academic English.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/single-case study with a very small sample (n=8) and no comparison group, randomization, or statistical analysis. The evidence is peer-reviewed and reasonably detailed, but credibility is limited by the design.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are encouraging, but they are based on a small ESL case study without an effect size and with outcomes that are largely descriptive. The impact is therefore modest and not clearly generalizable.

finding.finding_summary: In this case study of 8 ESL sixth-grade students, the engineering unit produced strong gains in engineering content knowledge as measured by a content-based final exam and hands-on circuit-building tasks. The class mean on the final exam was 82%, and all 8 students were able to independently build a circuit that lit a bulb and then modify it to make the bulb dimmer by inserting a resistor in series.
finding.measure: Content-based final exam; hands-on circuit-building performance

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the engineering activities also supported academic English development, especially vocabulary and oral explanation in an ESL setting. Students transitioned from shy, timid behavior to being more animated and confident in using spoken and written English, though no standardized language assessment or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Classroom participation, spoken/written English use, vocabulary acquisition

finding.finding_summary: The unit appears to have improved engagement and confidence among the ESL students. The author describes students as moving from shy and timid demeanors to vibrant, animated, and confident behaviors while participating in hands-on engineering tasks, but this is based on qualitative observation rather than a formal scale.
finding.measure: Observed student engagement, confidence, and enthusiasm
